BIT 5534 Applied Business Intelligence and Analytics
Week 10 · Lecture 1
Text Analytics with a Bag of Words
Duration: 75 minutes · Platform: Hokie AI · Submission: Thread exported as a .zip and uploaded to Canvas before leaving class · Lecture Mode: exploratory
Learning Objectives

By the end of this lecture, students will be able to:

  1. Turn a set of documents into a document term matrix of counts, and say what tokenizing and stop words remove.
  2. Compute df, idf and a tf-idf weight for a term, and explain why a rare term weighs more than a common one.
  3. Compute the cosine similarity of two documents from their tf-idf rows, and name what it can and cannot detect.
  4. Describe LSA and NMF as two factorizations of the same matrix, and read an NMF topic from its words.
  5. Compare PCA, t-SNE and UMAP maps of the same documents, and say what each map keeps.
  6. Name a kind of document a bag of words model would misplace, and the words that misplace it.
Section 1 of 5
INTRODUCTION
📋 Note for Students

Every model in this course so far has read columns of numbers. Most of what a business records is text: help desk tickets, reviews, emails, call notes, claims. Today turns text into columns with the oldest method that still works, the bag of words, and on Thursday we replace it with embeddings from a transformer model.

The case is Kestrel Point Outfitters, a made-up outdoor gear retailer with stores, a warehouse, an office and remote customer service agents. The names of the company, its stores and its people are made up. The tickets come from the company's own employees, whose registers, scanners, laptops and accounts are all supported by its IT help desk. The help desk received 600 tickets in one month. Each ticket has the text the employee typed, the site it came from, the queue the help desk put it in (account, network or hardware), whether it was escalated to a senior technician, and the hours it took to resolve.

A regression, a tree, a network and a support vector machine all read rows of numbers. A ticket is a string of words of any length. The bag of words turns each ticket into a row of the same length by forgetting the order of the words and keeping only how often each one appears.

Three steps make the row. Tokenizing lowercases the text and splits it into words, and here a word is two or more letters. Stop words, the most common words of English such as of, my, not and again, are dropped. Each remaining word becomes a column, called a term, and each ticket becomes a row holding how many times each term appears in it. The table of all rows is the document term matrix, the DTM.

The ticket matrix is almost all zeros. 600 tickets use 1235 terms that appear in at least two tickets, and the average ticket, about forty words long, fills seventeen of its 1235 cells. Of the 741,000 cells, 10,387 are not zero, 1.40 percent. The most common terms are the least informative ones, because a word that appears in every kind of ticket cannot tell one kind from another.

💬 Discussion

Before the weights:

  • The word not is a stop word. Name a ticket whose meaning reverses when not is dropped.
Section 2 of 5
DEMONSTRATION

A count treats every term the same. The term password in a ticket says more than the term morning, because password appears in fewer tickets. Inverse document frequency, idf, puts that into a number. df is how many tickets contain the term, and idf falls as df rises. Multiplying each count by its term's idf gives the tf-idf weight, and each ticket's row is then scaled to length 1 so that a long ticket and a short one are on the same footing.

Work d1. Accepted, account and locked appear in one of the four tickets, so each has idf ln(5/2) + 1 = 1.916. Password appears in two, so its idf is ln(5/3) + 1 = 1.511. The row's length is the square root of 3 times 1.916 squared plus 1.511 squared, 3.646, and dividing by it gives 0.525 for the rare terms and 0.414 for password. On the 600 tickets the same formula gives laptop, in 129 tickets, an idf of 2.53 and toner, in 9, an idf of 5.10.

Two tickets are similar when their rows point the same way. The cosine of the angle between two rows is their products summed over the terms, divided by both lengths, and because every tf-idf row already has length 1 it is just the sum of the products. It is 1 for two tickets with the same weights and 0 for two tickets that share no term.

The zero for a term two tickets do not share is the limit of the whole method. Forty three of the tickets are from a person who cannot sign in, written six different ways. In the heatmap each block is one wording, and the bright squares sit inside the blocks. Two sign in tickets with the same wording average a cosine of 0.213, two with different wordings average 0.046, and 45 percent of the pairs with different wordings share no term at all. To a bag of words, locked out and login error are unrelated.

A matrix with 1235 columns is too wide to read and too wide for a model fitted on 427 training tickets. Two factorizations shrink it. LSA, latent semantic analysis, applies the singular value decomposition to the tf-idf matrix without centering it, and keeps the first few components. On a centered matrix the same decomposition returns the principal components of week 4, so LSA is PCA on uncentered word weights. NMF, non-negative matrix factorization, writes the matrix as a product of two smaller matrices whose entries are all zero or positive. In NMF a ticket's row of W says how much of each topic it holds, and a topic's row of H says which terms make it up.

LSA 1 is not on the figure. Without centering, the first component points toward the average ticket, so its loadings are nearly all positive and it mostly says how much a ticket uses the common words. The components after it are the ones to read.

The last step draws each ticket as a point. PCA projects the tf-idf rows onto their two largest directions of spread, exactly as in week 4, so it keeps the large distances and blurs the small ones. t-SNE, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding, places points so that each one keeps its nearest neighbors close, and the gaps between groups mean little. UMAP, uniform manifold approximation and projection, also keeps each point's neighbors and keeps more of the arrangement between groups than t-SNE does. The figure draws all three on counts and on tf-idf, colored by the help desk's own category. The category was not an input to any of the three methods.

The tool, text_explorer.py, opens a window like the week 8 tools and works on any file with a column of text. You open the file, choose the text column, set the number of topics k and of LSA components, and press Run the analysis. It builds both matrices, the topics and the LSA components, draws the maps, and opens one page with four tabs, Map, Matrix, Words and Topics. Clicking a point on the map lists its five nearest tickets by cosine, with their shared terms marked. Save file with them writes your file with TOPIC_1 to TOPIC_k, LSA_1 to LSA_n and TEXT_terms added as numeric columns that the week 8 tools read.

Section 4 of 5
DISCUSSION

The queues were not an input to NMF, and three of its six topics line up with one queue almost completely. T1 mixes hardware and network because a broken register and a store whose registers cannot connect use the same words, register and store. T6 is built from open, computer, morning and drive, words about how people write a ticket more than about what went wrong.

💬 Discussion

Take these into the reflection:

  • T1 holds 54 network tickets. Which words put a network problem into a topic that is mostly hardware?
  • KP10031 found one sign in ticket among its five neighbors. What did the other four share with it, and would a help desk call that similar?

The new columns are inputs like any other. A logistic regression on the six topic weights alone reaches a validation AUC of 0.705 for escalation, against 0.558 for the site the ticket came from. On Thursday we test whether a model built on the meaning of a ticket does better than one built on its words.

💬 Discussion

One more:

  • Adding the site and the LSA columns to the six topics lowered the validation AUC from 0.705 to 0.692. What does that say about adding columns?

Turn to the person beside you for three minutes. Each of you names one topic you would trust to route tickets AND one you would not, with the words that decide it, from the Topics tab. A routing rule is only as good as the topics it rests on, and naming the weak one aloud is the first test of the reason.

Section 5 of 5
REFLECTION

Now write your reflection, in your own words and without help from the AI.

Your reflection needs all four of these. Give two terms from the Words tab with their df and idf, and say why one carries more weight in a ticket than the other AND say how many of the five tf-idf neighbors of KP10031 are from a person who cannot sign in, and which words tie the others to it AND name one topic in your own words, give its top words, and say which category most of its tickets come from AND say whether you would route tickets to the three queues by these six topics, naming one topic you would trust to route and one you would not, and saying why from their words. Respond to all four.

The fourth is where a good reflection separates from an adequate one. Either answer can be defended, and the defense rests on what the words of each topic describe.
